record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: How can memory encoding and erasing in soft glassy materials be controlled well enough to design conditioning protocols that do not bias later rheological experiments, and how are unrecoverable strain, stored memory, and readout methods such as orthogonal superposition rheometry connected?

evidence.quote: A better control of memory encoding and erasing is needed to design smarter conditioning protocols. Moving forward, future experiments need to delve deeper into establishing the connection between unrecoverable strain and memory storage. Moreover, efforts should be directed toward devising methods for the effective readout of stored memory , with a particular focus on employing orthogonal superposition rheometry .

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft glassy material (e.g., a dense colloidal suspension, microgel paste, emulsion, or foam) that can store mechanical "memory" of its deformation history. When such a material is subjected to a conditioning protocol — for instance, a sequence of pre-shears, oscillatory deformations, or rest periods — the resulting state generally biases subsequent rheological measurements. Decompose the total accumulated strain γ into a recoverable part γ_r (which relaxes upon removal of stress) and an unrecoverable part γ_u, and regard γ_u as a candidate scalar parameter encoding stored memory.

Address the following coupled questions:

1. (Encoding/erasing.) Identify deformation protocols (specified by waveform, amplitude, frequency, and rest history) that deterministically write a chosen memory into the material and, conversely, protocols that fully erase prior memory so that the post-conditioning state is statistically reproducible and does not bias later constitutive measurements.

2. (Unrecoverable strain ↔ stored memory.) Establish a quantitative relationship between the unrecoverable strain γ_u (or a functional thereof) and the stored memory content, including the conditions under which γ_u is a faithful one-to-one encoder of memory and the conditions under which additional state variables are required.

3. (Readout.) Design a readout scheme — in particular using orthogonal superposition rheometry, in which a small-amplitude oscillatory shear of frequency ω is applied perpendicular to a steady shear of rate γ̇₀, yielding a complex modulus G*⊥(ω; γ̇₀) — that recovers the stored memory non-destructively, and characterize how G*⊥(ω; γ̇₀) depends on γ_u and on the encoding protocol.

Give a framework or constitutive model that simultaneously answers (1)–(3) for a representative class of soft glassy materials.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) reports partial progress: rheo-XPCS experiments link recoverable/unrecoverable strain to microstructural memory in colloidal gels, and cyclic-shear studies of nanocolloidal glasses characterize training and memory. Orthogonal superposition rheometry has been used to probe jammed microgels and attractive glasses. However, no unified framework currently provides bias-free conditioning protocols, a complete mapping between unrecoverable strain and memory content, and a general OSR-based readout — the question remains open.

status_evidence.title: Linking structural and rheological memory in disordered soft materials
status_evidence.snippet: Connects transient structure and rheological memory via a generalized memory function; recoverable strain serves as a measure of nanoscale structural memory.
status_evidence.claim: Partial link between recoverable/unrecoverable strain and stored memory has been established experimentally.

status_evidence.title: Microstructural and rheological training and memory of nanocolloidal soft glasses under cyclic shear
status_evidence.snippet: Irreversible displacements in consecutive cycles become correlated at high amplitude, characterizing training and memory.
status_evidence.claim: Training/memory protocols are being characterized but not yet unified with a constitutive readout framework.

status_evidence.title: Orthogonal superposition rheometry of soft core–shell microgels
status_evidence.snippet: OSR superimposes small oscillatory shear orthogonal to steady shear to probe viscoelastic spectra of jammed microgels.
status_evidence.claim: OSR is an active but not fully developed memory-readout tool for soft glasses.
